Few medical developments have caught the attention of life actuaries as
quickly as GLP-1 drugs. Obesity is linked to seven of the ten leading causes
of death in high-income countries
([Swiss Re](https://www.swissre.com/press-release/GLP-1-drugs-may-reduce-mortality-by-up-to-6-4-in-the-US-by-2045/3f8ec083-2b76-4eea-88cb-e5af644e045d)),
so a class of drugs that reliably produces 15–20% weight loss could move
population mortality, and with it the experience of every life insurance and
annuity portfolio.

The impact is not symmetric. Lower mortality is **good news for protection
business** (term life, critical illness) but **a cost for longevity business**
(annuities, pensions, pension risk transfer). In this post I look at:

1. how GLP-1 drugs evolved,
2. what the evidence shows so far, and where it is still weak,
3. what reinsurers project for the US, Canada and the UK, and
4. what this could mean, in numbers, for protection and longevity products.

## How GLP-1 drugs evolved

GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) is a gut hormone released after eating. It
stimulates insulin, slows stomach emptying and signals fullness to the brain.
The challenge was turning it into a drug: natural GLP-1 is cleared from the
body within minutes
([Lasker Foundation / JCI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11446598/)).

| Period | Milestone |
|---|---|
| **1980s** | GLP-1 identified by Joel Habener's group and Svetlana Mojsov; Lotte Bjerre Knudsen at Novo Nordisk later leads the work on long-acting versions. The three received the 2024 Lasker Award ([JCI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11446598/)). |
| **2005** | Exenatide, based on a peptide found in Gila monster venom, becomes the first GLP-1 drug approved for type 2 diabetes. |
| **2010–2014** | Liraglutide: daily injection for diabetes (Victoza), then for obesity (Saxenda). |
| **2017–2021** | Semaglutide: weekly injection for diabetes (Ozempic, 2017), then for obesity (Wegovy, 2021). |
| **2022–2023** | Tirzepatide, a dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist: Mounjaro (diabetes), Zepbound (obesity). **SELECT** shows a 20% cut in major cardiovascular events. |
| **2025** | Oral semaglutide for obesity (Wegovy pill) approved in the US in December; Swiss Re and RGA publish mortality projections. |
| **2026** | Canada approves the first generic semaglutide (April); Lilly's oral orforglipron (Foundayo) approved in the US (April); Medicare starts covering obesity drugs (July); triple-agonist retatrutide delivers up to 28% weight loss in phase 3. |

Each generation of injectable drugs has delivered more weight loss. The new
pills trade some of that efficacy for convenience: no injections, and (for
orforglipron) no food or water restrictions.

```{r}
#| label: fig-weight
#| fig-cap: "Mean weight loss in the drug arm of key phase 3 obesity trials (highest dose). Trials differ in population, duration and statistical method, so this is not a head-to-head comparison."
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
blue <- "#06436e"

trials <- tribble(
  ~drug,                           ~trial,                 ~loss, ~form,
  "Liraglutide 3.0 mg",            "SCALE, 56 wk",           8.0, "Injection",
  "Orforglipron 36 mg",            "ATTAIN-1, 72 wk",       11.2, "Pill",
  "Oral semaglutide 25 mg",        "OASIS 4, 64 wk",        13.6, "Pill",
  "Semaglutide 2.4 mg",            "STEP 1, 68 wk",         14.9, "Injection",
  "Tirzepatide 15 mg",             "SURMOUNT-1, 72 wk",     20.9, "Injection",
  "Retatrutide 12 mg (not yet approved)", "TRIUMPH-1, 80 wk",      28.3, "Injection"
) |>
  mutate(label = paste0(drug, "\n", trial),
         label = factor(label, levels = label[order(loss)]))

ggplot(trials, aes(loss, label, fill = form)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", loss)), hjust = -0.15, size = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Injection = blue, Pill = "#6cb6ec")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 32), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(x = "Mean body-weight reduction", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

Sources: SCALE, STEP 1, SURMOUNT-1 and OASIS 4 (published trial results);
ATTAIN-1 ([ACC summary of NEJM paper](https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/journal-scans/2025/09/24/16/48/attain-1));
TRIUMPH-1 ([Lilly](https://investor.lilly.com/news-releases/news-release-details/lillys-triple-agonist-retatrutide-successful-two-additional),
[Pharmacy Times](https://www.pharmacytimes.com/view/retatrutide-delivers-bariatric-level-weight-loss-pivotal-phase-3-triumph-1-trial)).

## The evidence so far

For an actuary, weight loss is only a proxy. What matters is whether people
**die less**, and whether the effect **lasts in the real world**. The evidence
comes in three layers.

### 1. Randomised trials with hard outcomes

| Trial | Population | Key result |
|---|---|---|
| **SELECT** (semaglutide, 2023) | 17,604 adults with overweight/obesity and established cardiovascular disease, **no diabetes**, ~40 months | Major cardiovascular events 6.5% vs 8.0%: a **20% relative reduction**. All-cause death HR 0.81 (secondary endpoint) (Lincoff et al., NEJM 2023; [Cleveland Clinic](https://newsroom.clevelandclinic.org/2023/11/11/international-clinical-trial-finds-that-semaglutide-reduced-cardiovascular-events-by-20-in-adults-with-overweight-or-obesity-who-dont-have-diabetes/)) |
| **FLOW** (semaglutide, 2024) | 3,533 adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease | Kidney outcomes HR 0.76; **all-cause death HR 0.80** (13% vs 16%); stopped early for efficacy ([ACC](https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/clinical-trials/2024/05/29/17/23/flow)) |
| **SURPASS-CVOT** (tirzepatide vs dulaglutide, 2025) | Adults with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease | Cardiovascular events HR 0.92 vs an *active* GLP-1 comparator (non-inferior); lower all-cause death ([Healio](https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinology/20250919/tirzepatide-similar-to-dulaglutide-for-cv-outcomes-but-tied-to-lower-rates-of-death)) |

These are the strongest pieces of evidence: a 20% reduction in all-cause
mortality, in two independent trials, in high-risk groups.

There are also clear **negative results**. In November 2025, the EVOKE trials
found that oral semaglutide did **not** slow Alzheimer's disease progression
([Alzheimer Europe](https://www.alzheimer-europe.org/news/results-evoke-and-evoke-trials-show-no-effect-oral-semaglutide-ad-progression)).
GLP-1s are not a cure-all, and benefits outside cardiometabolic disease
should not be assumed.

### 2. Real-world insured data

Munich Re analysed a US dataset of **41 million lives** with prescription and
mortality data from 2015 to January 2025
([Munich Re, February 2026](https://www.munichre.com/us-life/en/insights/clinical-knowledge/glp-1-therapies-and-mortality-risk-implications-for-life-insurers.html)):

- GLP-1 users had lower all-cause mortality than non-users, both **with and
  without diabetes**, with similar reductions in each group.
- The benefit was consistent under age 60 and **less pronounced above 60**.
- It held across income bands, including the moderate-to-affluent incomes
  typical of insured populations.
- Munich Re estimates GLP-1s may drive **0.2%–0.5% additional mortality
  improvement per year, over 20 years**.

### 3. Population-level signals

In the US, the share of adults currently taking a GLP-1 for weight loss rose
from **3% in 2024 to 11% in 2026**, and the adult obesity rate fell from a
peak of **39.9% in 2022 to 36.8% in 2026**
([Gallup](https://news.gallup.com/poll/712157/glp-usage-reaches-new-high.aspx)).
Gallup does not claim causation, but this is the first sustained fall in US
obesity in decades.

### The weak spot: persistence

The biggest uncertainty is not whether the drugs work, but whether people
**stay on them**:

- A meta-analysis of about 446,000 patients found **48.7% stop within one
  year**, with higher rates in people without diabetes
  ([Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, 2025](https://www.epocrates.com/online/contextuallink/article/higher-discontinuation-rates-of-glp-1-receptor-agonists-in-non-diabetic)).
- Only **1 in 12** people starting a GLP-1 for obesity (without diabetes) was
  still on it after three years
  ([Prime Therapeutics](https://www.biospace.com/press-releases/prime-therapeutics-leading-research-shows-only-1-in-12-remain-on-a-glp-1-drug-for-obesity-at-three-years)).
- In Munich Re's data, fewer than **30%** of non-diabetic users aged 30–40
  stayed on the drug beyond a year.
- Stopping usually means **regaining weight**: one year after stopping
  semaglutide in STEP 1, participants had regained about **two-thirds** of the
  weight they lost, and their cardiometabolic improvements reverted similarly
  ([STEP 1 extension](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9542252/)).

Persistence has improved as shortages eased and prices fell, and pills may
help further. But it remains the key assumption in every projection below.

## Projected impact: what reinsurers expect

Three major reinsurers have published quantitative projections:

| Study | Market | Impact on all-cause mortality by ~2045 |
|---|---|---|
| **Swiss Re** (Sept 2025) | US | 2.3% (pessimistic) to **6.4%** (optimistic) |
| | UK | 1.8% to **5.1%** |
| **RGA** (Nov 2025) | US | 1.0% / **3.5%** / 8.8% (pessimistic / central / optimistic) |
| | Canada | **2.6%** (central) |
| | UK | **2.0%** (central) |
| **Munich Re** (Feb 2026) | US | 0.2%–0.5% extra improvement **per year** for 20 years, roughly **4%–10%** cumulative (my conversion) |

Sources: [Swiss Re](https://www.swissre.com/press-release/GLP-1-drugs-may-reduce-mortality-by-up-to-6-4-in-the-US-by-2045/3f8ec083-2b76-4eea-88cb-e5af644e045d) and
[Reinsurance News](https://www.reinsurancene.ws/glp-1-drugs-could-cut-mortality-rates-in-us-and-uk-swiss-re-says/);
[RGA](https://www.rgare.com/knowledge-center/article/rga-glp-1-study--weighing-the-evidence);
[Munich Re](https://www.munichre.com/us-life/en/insights/clinical-knowledge/glp-1-therapies-and-mortality-risk-implications-for-life-insurers.html).

```{r}
#| label: fig-projections
#| fig-cap: "Projected reduction in population all-cause mortality by about 2045. Bars show each study's range; dots show central scenarios where published. Munich Re's range is converted from its annual figures."
proj <- tribble(
  ~study,      ~market,  ~low, ~central, ~high,
  "Swiss Re",  "US",      2.3,  NA,       6.4,
  "Swiss Re",  "UK",      1.8,  NA,       5.1,
  "RGA",       "US",      1.0,  3.5,      8.8,
  "RGA",       "Canada",  NA,   2.6,      NA,
  "RGA",       "UK",      NA,   2.0,      NA,
  "Munich Re", "US",      100 * (1 - 0.998^20), NA, 100 * (1 - 0.995^20)
) |>
  mutate(label = factor(paste(study, "·", market),
                        levels = rev(paste(study, "·", market))))

p_proj <- ggplot(proj, aes(y = label)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high), linewidth = 6,
                 colour = blue, alpha = 0.35, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(aes(x = central), size = 4, colour = blue, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_text(aes(x = central, label = sprintf("%.1f%%", central)), vjust = -1.2,
            size = 3.6, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 10.5), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(x = "Reduction in all-cause mortality by ~2045", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
p_proj
```

```{r}
#| label: thumbnail
#| include: false
ggsave("thumbnail.png", p_proj, width = 7, height = 4, dpi = 100, bg = "white")
```

Why do the numbers differ? Each model combines the same four ingredients, and
small changes in any of them compound:

- **Uptake:** how many people with obesity take the drugs.
- **Effectiveness:** how much weight they lose, and how much mortality falls
  per unit of weight lost (or beyond it, as SELECT suggests).
- **Persistence and rebound:** how long they stay on treatment, and how much
  of the benefit is lost when they stop.
- **Time to effect:** cardiovascular benefits appear within a few years;
  cancer benefits, if any, take much longer.

Three findings recur across the studies:

- **The effect is largest in middle age.** RGA finds the biggest reductions at
  ages 45–59 and the smallest at 85+, where uptake is lower and fewer deaths
  are cardiovascular. Munich Re sees the same pattern either side of age 60.
- **Insured lives benefit less than the general population.** They have a lower
  average BMI, so there is less room for improvement, which outweighs their
  better access to drugs (RGA).
- **Morbidity effects are smaller than mortality effects.** Cancer is the
  largest cause of critical illness claims, and BMI reduction lowers cancer
  risk less than it lowers cardiovascular risk (RGA).

## Market by market

### United States

The US has the highest obesity rate (around 40% of adults) and the fastest
uptake, and access is widening quickly:

- **Price and coverage.** In November 2025, the administration agreed lower
  prices with Lilly and Novo Nordisk, including direct-to-consumer sales
  through TrumpRx ([CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/11/06/trump-eli-lilly-novo-nordisk-deal-obesity-drug-prices.html)).
  Since **1 July 2026**, eligible Medicare beneficiaries can get obesity
  GLP-1s for a **$50 monthly copay** under a temporary "Bridge" program
  ([CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/30/medicare-obesity-drug-glp-1-coverage-starting-july-1.html)),
  ahead of the CMS **BALANCE** model in Part D from January 2027
  ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaid-coverage-of-and-spending-on-glp-1s/)).
- **Pills.** The Wegovy pill launched in January 2026, and Lilly's Foundayo
  (orforglipron) was approved on 1 April 2026; it needs no injection and has
  no food or water restrictions
  ([BioSpace](https://www.biospace.com/fda/eli-lillys-oral-obesity-pill-approved-kicking-off-renewed-novo-rivalry)).

**Protection:** a meaningful tailwind for term life, especially in the
45–59 age band where face amounts are high. Medicare coverage matters less
for protection than for longevity, since it targets people aged 65+.

**Longevity:** cheaper access for over-65s via Medicare increases the
relevance for annuities and pension risk transfer, although the effect at the
oldest ages is expected to be smallest.

### Canada

Canada is the **first G7 country with generic semaglutide**. Novo Nordisk did
not maintain its Canadian patent, and Health Canada approved the first generic
in April 2026
([Health Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/news/2026/04/canada-becomes-the-first-g7-country-to-approve-a-generic-version-of-semaglutide.html)),
followed by the first generic for weight management (Apotex's Sevmia) in June
([Health Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/news/2026/06/canada-approves-first-generic-semaglutide-for-weight-loss.html))
and further approvals since, including Sandoz in September
([Pearce IP](https://www.pearceip.law/2026/09/18/sandozs-generic-ozempic-semaglutide-approved-in-canada/)).

- RGA's central projection for Canada is a **2.6%** mortality reduction by
  2045, between the US and UK.
- Generic prices could push uptake towards the **optimistic** end of the
  range, making Canada a natural experiment for the whole industry.
- Munich Re's Canadian team expects underwriting to improve and
  **insurability to expand**: more applicants qualifying for standard or
  preferred rates
  ([Digital Insurance](https://www.dig-in.com/news/munich-re-how-glp-1-and-ai-impact-life-insurance)).
- For **group benefits**, wider use of cheaper generics shifts the cost
  pressure on drug plans.

### United Kingdom

In the UK, **private** use runs well ahead of the NHS:

- NHS England is rolling out Mounjaro to about **220,000 people over three
  years**, starting with those with a BMI above 40 and at least four related
  conditions. Access is uneven: by one BMJ analysis, fewer than half of
  commissioning bodies had started prescribing.
- An estimated **1.5 million or more** people use weight-loss drugs, around
  nine in ten paying privately (estimates vary)
  ([UK reporting](https://earlsdonpharmacy.co.uk/weight-loss-injections-nhs/)).
- Lilly raised the UK private list price of Mounjaro by up to **170%** from
  September 2025, which may reduce persistence among private users
  ([PharmExec](https://www.pharmexec.com/view/eli-lilly-170-percent-price-increase-mounjaro-uk)).

**Protection:** Swiss Re projects a 1.8%–5.1% mortality reduction and RGA
2.0% (central): smaller than the US because obesity is lower (around 30% of
adults) and NHS access is restricted.

**Longevity:** this is where the UK stands out. With one of the largest bulk
annuity markets in the world, small changes in improvement assumptions move
billions. Yet a Standard Life survey found that **69% of defined benefit
trustees had not yet considered** the effect of these drugs on life
expectancy
([Standard Life](https://www.standardlifeplc.com/news-and-views/press-releases/article-page/health-innovations-may-trigger-longevity-challenge)).
The CMI_2025 projections model (March 2026) has no separate GLP-1 component;
users can express their views through parameters such as the long-term rate
of improvement
([IFoA](https://actuaries.org.uk/news/cmi-publishes-cmi_2025-mortality-projections-model/)).

## Protection versus longevity: an illustration

How big are these effects for actual products? Here is a simple illustration
in the spirit of my
[previous post on mortality improvement](../mortality-improvement-lee-carter/index.qmd).
I take England & Wales male death rates as a base table and apply a GLP-1
mortality reduction that phases in linearly from 2027 to 2045 and stays
constant after that. I then compare, against no GLP-1 effect:

- **Protection:** the expected cost of a 20-year term life policy sold to a
  45-year-old (pays 1 on death, 3% interest).
- **Longevity:** the value of a life annuity of 1 per year for a 65-year-old
  (3% interest, to age 100).

I test two age patterns: a **uniform** reduction at all ages, and a
**tapered** one closer to the evidence (full effect below 60, reducing to 30%
of the effect at 85 and above).

```{r}
#| label: illustration
library(StMoMo)

ages <- 45:100
base <- (EWMaleData$Dxt / EWMaleData$Ext)[as.character(ages), "2011"]

# Share of the headline reduction applying at each age
taper <- pmin(1, pmax(0.3, 1 - 0.7 * (ages - 60) / 25))
names(taper) <- ages

# Death rate at age x in projection year k (k = 1 is 2027, k = 19 is 2045)
rate <- function(x, k, r, tapered) {
  w <- if (tapered) taper[as.character(x)] else 1
  base[as.character(x)] * (1 - r * w * min(k / 19, 1))
}

term_cost <- function(r, tapered = FALSE, age0 = 45, n = 20, i = 0.03) {
  q  <- sapply(0:(n - 1), function(k) 1 - exp(-rate(age0 + k, k + 1, r, tapered)))
  kp <- c(1, cumprod(1 - q))[1:n]          # survival to start of each year
  sum(kp * q * (1 + i)^-(1:n))
}

annuity <- function(r, tapered = FALSE, age0 = 65, i = 0.03) {
  n  <- 100 - age0 + 1
  q  <- sapply(0:(n - 1), function(k) 1 - exp(-rate(age0 + k, k + 1, r, tapered)))
  sum(cumprod(1 - q) * (1 + i)^-(1:n))
}

scenarios <- tibble(
  Scenario = c("RGA pessimistic (US)", "RGA central (US)",
               "Swiss Re optimistic (US)", "RGA optimistic (US)"),
  r = c(0.010, 0.035, 0.064, 0.088)
)

results <- scenarios |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    term_u = term_cost(r) / term_cost(0) - 1,
    ann_u  = annuity(r) / annuity(0) - 1,
    ann_t  = annuity(r, TRUE) / annuity(0, TRUE) - 1
  ) |>
  ungroup()

pct <- function(x) sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * x)
results |>
  transmute(
    Scenario,
    `Mortality reduction by 2045` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * r),
    `20-year term cost, age 45` = pct(term_u),
    `Annuity value, age 65 (uniform)` = pct(ann_u),
    `Annuity value, age 65 (tapered)` = pct(ann_t)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lcccc")
```

A few takeaways:

- **The effects look small, but they are not.** In the central scenario, the
  term policy becomes about
  `r sprintf("%.1f%%", -100 * results$term_u[2])` cheaper, and the annuity
  about `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * results$ann_t[2])` more expensive with the
  tapered age pattern. On a large in-force annuity book, a fraction of a
  percent of reserves is a material amount of capital.
- **Protection captures only part of the benefit.** A policy sold today runs
  mostly during the phase-in years, before the full effect is reached.
- **The age pattern matters a lot for annuities.** With the tapered pattern,
  the annuity impact is roughly
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - results$ann_t[2] / results$ann_u[2]))`
  smaller than with a uniform reduction, because annuity cash flows sit at the
  ages where the evidence for benefit is weakest.
- **Insured lives would see less.** These figures use population-level
  reductions; RGA and Munich Re both expect smaller effects for insured lives.

This is deliberately simple: one base table, no background improvement, and
the reinsurers' population-level figures applied directly. But it shows the
asymmetry clearly.

## Implications for underwriting

GLP-1s also change **who** buys insurance, and **how** they look at
underwriting:

- **Anti-selection risk.** An applicant who has recently lost weight on a
  GLP-1 may qualify for a better rating class, then stop treatment and regain
  the weight. Given the persistence data, this is a real concern.
- **Accelerated underwriting** relies on self-reported height and weight and
  may misclassify recent GLP-1 users more often than full underwriting
  ([Celent](https://www.celent.com/insights/weightloss)).
- **Better data helps.** Prescription histories and electronic health records
  can show when treatment started and whether it continued (Munich Re).
  Underwriters increasingly look at weight *before* treatment and at
  treatment duration, not just current BMI.
- **Expanding insurability.** For applicants who stay on treatment, improved
  blood pressure, glucose and lipid profiles are real risk reductions. Some
  previously declined or rated applicants may become insurable.
- **Fraud.** With pills and online prescribing, insurers will need to verify
  that disclosed treatment is genuine
  ([Insurance Business](https://www.insurancebusinessmag.com/uk/news/life-insurance/foundayo-launch-puts-glp1-pill-fraud-risk-on-brokers-radar-587134.aspx)).

## What to watch next

- **Persistence in newer cohorts**, as prices fall and pills become available.
- **Canada's generic market**: the first real test of what cheap,
  widely available semaglutide does to uptake.
- **Medicare uptake**: how many over-65s start treatment, which matters most
  for longevity risk.
- **Next-generation drugs**: Lilly plans to submit retatrutide for approval
  in the first quarter of 2027.
- **Insured experience studies**: cause-of-death trends in insured
  portfolios, split by age, will be the clearest signal for pricing and
  reserving.

## My take

The evidence that GLP-1 drugs reduce mortality in high-risk groups is now
strong: two randomised trials show about a 20% reduction in all-cause death,
and real-world data point in the same direction. What is **not** yet known is
how much of that benefit survives real-world persistence, and how it spreads
across a whole population over 20 years.

For **protection** business, this is an upside to monitor rather than to
price in early, with the bigger near-term issue being underwriting. For
**longevity** business, it is a risk that deserves explicit scenario testing
now, especially in the UK, where the stakes are large and many pension
trustees have not yet considered it. As RGA put it, it may be too early to
make material changes to trend assumptions, but the direction of travel is
clear.
